reagents.name: Iron(III) chloride solution, 0.5 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid iron(III) chloride hexahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H302: Harmful if swallowed
H315: Causes skin irritation
H318: Causes serious eye damage

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L, which is about 8% iron(III) chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier has no sheet for a solution of this strength: one of its sheets is for iron(III) chloride solutions of 0.1 M or less and the next is for 1 M to 2.3 M, and this solution lies between the two. So this note rests on the stricter of them, the sheet for 1 M to 2.3 M, and this solution is handled as that sheet says. It gives the signal word Warning and three statements: under H303, that the solution may be harmful if swallowed; under H316, that it causes mild irritation of the skin; and under H319, that it seriously irritates the eyes. The sheet for 0.1 M or less also gives Warning, with two statements: H316 again, and for the eyes H320, irritation that it does not call serious. Each sheet gives its solution a pH of about 1. Both call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. Both say that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that medical advice is to be sought if the eyes stay irritated or the skin becomes irritated. Both also ask for flushing with water at once, kept up for 15 minutes or more, without saying whether that is for the skin or for the eyes.

reagents.name: Sodium hydroxide solution, 1 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium hydroxide, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value: The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L, which is about 4% sodium hydroxide by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's sheet for sodium hydroxide solutions of 0.3 M to 6.0 M, which covers this strength, gives the signal word Danger and one statement, under the code H314: the solution burns the skin severely and damages the eyes. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and says that the mist, the vapour or the spray of the solution is not to be breathed. It says that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up. After a splash on the skin or the hair, it says, the wet clothing is to come off at once and the skin be rinsed with water.

reagents.name: Copper(II) sulfate solution, 0.5 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H301: Toxic if swallowed
H315+H319: Causes skin and serious eye irritation

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L, which is between 7% and 8% copper(II) sulfate by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). reagents.name: Nickel(II) chloride solution, 0.5 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid nickel(II) chloride hexahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H301+H331: Toxic if swallowed or inhaled
H315: Causes skin irritation
H317+H334: May cause an allergic skin reaction, allergy or asthma symptoms or breathing difficulties if inhaled
H341: Suspected of causing genetic defects
H350: May cause cancer
H360: May damage fertility or the unborn child
H372: Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L, which is about 6% nickel(II) chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's one sheet for a solution of nickel chloride in water does not reach this strength: its table of composition stops at 3% of the hexahydrate, and this solution holds about 12 g of the hexahydrate in each 100 mL, some four times as much. Even so, that sheet gives the signal word Danger and five statements: under H303, that its solution may be harmful if swallowed; under H316, that it causes mild irritation of the skin; under H350, that it may cause cancer; under H360, that it may harm fertility or an unborn child; and under H372, that it damages organs in a person exposed to it for a long time or again and again. With no sheet for a solution this concentrated, handle this one as the sheet for the solid says, whose statements are those above. Besides the last three of those five, the solid's sheet says that the substance is toxic if it is swallowed or breathed in (H301 and H331), that it irritates the skin (H315), that it may set off an allergy of the skin, or asthma or trouble with breathing if it is breathed in (H317 and H334), and that it is suspected of doing damage to the genes (H341). The solid's sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, for work in a fume hood or a well-ventilated room, and for breathing protection, and says that clothing the substance has got onto is not to leave the workplace. It says that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called by anyone who has been exposed to the substance or is worried that they have. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that medical advice is to be sought if the eyes stay irritated. Skin is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, it says, and medical advice sought if the skin becomes irritated or a rash appears. If the substance is swallowed, the mouth is to be rinsed and a poison centre or a doctor called at once.

reagents.name: Magnesium ribbon
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of magnesium metal, as turnings or ribbon, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H228: Flammable solid

note.value: The magnesium on this bench is a short piece of ribbon. The supplier's sheet for magnesium, which is for the metal as turnings or ribbon, gives the signal word Danger and one statement, under the code H228: the metal is a solid that burns readily. The sheet says to keep it away from flames, sparks, heat and hot surfaces. It says that burning magnesium is put out with dry sand or with an extinguisher of class D, and never with water, with which it reacts violently. It lists water and acids among the things the metal is to be kept from; at this bench a short piece is put into acid on purpose, as the experiment. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. It says that eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that skin is to be washed with plenty of water. In its section on toxicology it calls the dust of the metal irritating.

solutionHeatCapacity.note: The specific heat of water, used for every mixed solution: an idealisation (spec 5.2). The section prints the figure to four digits, 4.184, and once as 4.18 in a worked example; the three-figure value is stored. The difference moves a computed temperature rise by a tenth of a percent.

solutionDensity.note: The density of water, used for every mixed solution: an idealisation (spec 5.2). The mass that warms is taken as the volume of the liquid times this figure; a solid or a metal added to it is left out.

warmFromC.rationale: A computed temperature rise of at least this many degrees Celsius is recorded as warm. Chosen so that the magnesium tube, which the model warms by about 11 °C, is warm to the touch, and so that a rise too small to feel in a test tube reads as no change.

hotFromC.rationale: A computed temperature rise of at least this many degrees Celsius is recorded as hot. Chosen so that the tube of 6 M acid and 6 M base, which the model warms by about 40 °C to some 60 °C or more, is hot, and the magnesium tube is not.

sniffing.value: Do not put your nose over a tube and breathe in. A guide to safe practice in laboratories says that sniffing a chemical is in general not encouraged, that it is done only where a procedure calls for it and the substance has been checked beforehand, and that a toxic or unknown substance is never sniffed on purpose. Where a procedure does call for it, the vapour is wafted gently towards the nose. Use the waft tool.

hotTube.value: Careful: this tube is hot, and what went into it is corrosive. The acid and the base are each strong enough to burn skin and damage eyes, and a real tube never holds exactly equal amounts of the two, so the mixture may still be strongly acidic or strongly basic. Do not close your hand around the tube: touch the outside briefly, or use the thermometer.

stations.name: Iron(III) chloride and sodium hydroxide
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube once the two solutions are mixed: two from each bottle.
Pair each positive ion with the negative ion that came from the other bottle, and look each pair up in the solubility table.

An iron(III) ion carries three positive charges and a hydroxide ion one negative charge. How many hydroxide ions does one iron(III) ion need? Is there enough hydroxide in the tube for all of the iron?

notes.value: The solid is written Fe(OH)₃ here, as it usually is. What settles out of a real tube is better described as a hydrated iron(III) oxide: iron, oxygen and water, in no fixed proportion.

stations.name: Sodium carbonate and copper(II) sulfate
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube once the two solutions are mixed: two from each bottle.
Pair each positive ion with the negative ion that came from the other bottle, and look each pair up in the solubility table.
The blue of the copper(II) sulfate solution belongs to one of its two ions. If the liquid ends up colourless, where has that ion gone?

notes.value: The equation checked here is the simple carbonate: Cu²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CuCO₃. The solid that really forms when these two solutions meet is a basic carbonate, which holds hydroxide as well as carbonate, such as Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃. The blue-green recorded here is that solid's colour. Plain CuCO₃ is hard to make at all.

stations.name: Sodium carbonate and nickel(II) chloride
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube once the two solutions are mixed: two from each bottle.
Pair each positive ion with the negative ion that came from the other bottle, and look each pair up in the solubility table.
Count the chloride ions: one NiCl₂ gives two. They have to be balanced on the other side of the equation as well.

notes.value: The equation checked here is the simple carbonate: Ni²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → NiCO₃. As with copper, the solid that really forms from a nickel salt solution and sodium carbonate is a basic carbonate, with hydroxide in it as well as carbonate.

stations.name: Barium chloride and copper(II) sulfate
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube once the two solutions are mixed: two from each bottle.
Pair each positive ion with the negative ion that came from the other bottle, and look each pair up in the solubility table.
The liquid is still blue after the solid has formed. Which ion gives it that colour, and has anything happened to that ion?

stations.name: Cobalt(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube. Both bottles hold a chloride.
A solid needs a positive ion and a negative ion that are insoluble together. How many different negative ions are there here, and what does the solubility table say of each pairing?

notes.value: Nothing reacts here. The only negative ion in the tube is chloride, and cobalt(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride both dissolve, so no pairing of these ions makes a solid, and there is no acid, base or metal for anything else to happen. The two colours only blend. The answer to all three equations is "No reaction".

stations.name: Ammonium nitrate and sodium hydroxide
hints: No solid forms here, so look for another sign. One of the ions in the tube is a weak acid and another is a strong base.
When an ammonium ion gives a hydrogen ion to a hydroxide ion, what is left of the ammonium ion, and what has the hydroxide ion become?
Ammonia and water are molecules, not ions. Write each as a whole formula in every equation.

notes.value: Red litmus dipped into the liquid turns blue, but that proves nothing about ammonia: there is sodium hydroxide left over in the tube, and it would turn the paper blue with no ammonium nitrate there at all. Moist red litmus held above the liquid, touching neither the liquid nor the glass, turns blue only if a basic gas reaches it. That gas is ammonia.
Do not expect to see the gas bubbling out: ammonia is very soluble in water, and most of it stays dissolved. The smell and the litmus held in the vapour are the signs.

stations.name: Calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid
hints: The white powder is a solid that does not dissolve in water, so it is not split into ions: it goes into every equation as one formula.
Each carbonate takes two hydrogen ions from the acid. Is there enough acid in the tube for all of the powder?
The gas contains the carbon of the carbonate.

stations.name: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, both 6 M
hints: Nothing changes to the eye. A reaction can also show itself by heat.
An acid gives hydrogen ions and a base gives hydroxide ions. What do one of each make together?
Water is a molecule and a liquid: write it as a whole formula.

notes.value: There is nothing to see: both solutions are colourless, and so is the solution of salt they make. Heat is the only sign that anything has happened. The temperature rise worked out for this tube is idealised: it assumes that no heat escapes and that the liquid warms as easily as plain water, so a real tube gets somewhat less hot.

stations.name: Cobalt(II) chloride and silver nitrate
hints: Write down every ion that is in the tube once the two solutions are mixed: two from each bottle.
Pair each positive ion with the negative ion that came from the other bottle, and look each pair up in the solubility table.
The silver nitrate solution is much weaker than the cobalt(II) chloride solution. Which ion runs out first, and which ions are left over in the liquid?

stations.name: Magnesium and hydrochloric acid
hints: The ribbon is a metal, a solid: it goes into every equation as one formula, with no charge.
The metal ends up dissolved, as an ion with two positive charges. Something else must have taken up the charge it gave away.
The gas is an element whose molecules hold two atoms.
